verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — RETENTION PERIOD UNDER DIRECTIVE 2014/32/EU (MID)

1. ANSWER

Ten (10) years. A manufacturer must keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the measuring instrument has been placed on the market.

2. LEGAL BASIS

Article 8(3), Directive 2014/32/EU (Chapter 2, 'Obligations of economic operators' — Obligations of manufacturers):

  '3. Manufacturers shall keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after the measuring instrument has been placed on the market.'

Source text (adopted version, reproducing OJ L 96, 29.3.2014): legislation.gov.uk, EUDR 2014/32, Chapter 2, plain extent.

The same 10-year period is reproduced in the module provisions of the instrument-specific annexes. Verified example, Annex II:

  Point 5.2: 'The manufacturer shall draw up a written EU declaration of conformity for each instrument model and keep it at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market... A copy of the EU declaration of conformity shall be supplied with each measuring instrument that is placed on the market. However, this requirement may be interpreted as applying to a batch or consignment rather than individual instruments in those cases where a large number of instruments is delivered to a single user.'

  Point 6: 'The manufacturer shall, for a period ending 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market, keep at the disposal of the national authorities: (a) the technical documentation referred to in point 3.1; (b) the documentation concerning the quality system referred to in point 3.1; (c) the information relating to the change referred to in point 3.5, as approved; (d) the decisions and reports from the notified body referred to in points 3.5, 4.3 and 4.4.'

3. VERSION IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21 — VERIFICATION

(a) Original instrument: the 2014 OJ text (CELEX 32014L0032) states 10 years at Article 8(3).
(b) Consolidated text: EUR-Lex consolidation CELEX 02014L0032-20281010 — a consolidation incorporating amendments applicable from 10 October 2028, i.e. a text later in time than the material date — still states 10 years at Article 8(3) and at Annex II points 5.2 and 6.
(c) The material date 2026-11-21 therefore sits inside an interval whose lower end (2014 original) and upper end (2028 consolidation) both prescribe 10 years. The determination does not depend on which consolidation is used.
(d) Known intervening amendment: Regulation (EU) 2019/1243 amended Article 47 (delegated-act machinery) and does not touch Article 8.
(e) Residual, non-blocking verification step: a check of EUR-Lex's 'all consolidated versions' list for 2014–2026 to exclude a transient amendment that changed Article 8(3) and was later reversed. No such amendment is known and the bracketing in (c) makes the risk negligible.

4. SCOPE POINTS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE NUMBER

(a) Instrument category. Article 8 is horizontal and applies to every measuring instrument within the Directive's scope (instrument-specific Annexes MI-001 to MI-011). The annexes reproduce the same 10 years in their module provisions, so the answer is 10 years whichever conformity-assessment module (B+F, B+D, G, H1, etc.) was used. No category-specific shorter or longer period exists in the Directive.
(b) Start of the clock. The period runs from the date the individual instrument is placed on the market, not from the date the declaration was drawn up or the model designed. For a series produced over years the period is instrument-by-instrument; serial/lot-level placing-on-market dates must be recorded.
(c) Same period for both documents. Article 8(3) covers the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity in a single sentence. Annex II point 6 extends the same 10 years to the quality-system documentation, the approved change information and the notified body's decisions and reports.
(d) 'Placed on the market' vs 'put into use'. The retention trigger in Article 8(3) is placing on the market (first making available on the Union market). A later putting into use neither restarts nor shortens the clock; a later amendment of the Directive does not shorten the tail for instruments already placed on the market.
(e) Parallel duties of other operators. Article 9(2)(a): an authorised representative's written mandate must allow it to keep the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation at the disposal of national market surveillance authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market. Article 10(8): importers must keep a copy of the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the market surveillance authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market and ensure the technical documentation can be made available on request. These duties are additional to, and do not discharge, the manufacturer's own Article 8(3) duty. Distributors have no equivalent retention duty under Article 11.

5. PROCEDURE — WHAT 'KEEP AT THE DISPOSAL OF THE NATIONAL AUTHORITIES' REQUIRES

Step 1 — Date capture. Record, per instrument or per serial range/batch, the date it is first placed on the market (invoice/first transfer date to an independent operator in the Union).

Step 2 — File assembly, per instrument model: (i) technical documentation per Article 18 / Annex II point 3.1 (design and manufacture data, risk and conformity assessment evidence, test reports); (ii) the EU declaration of conformity (one per instrument model); (iii) notified body certificates, decisions and reports; (iv) quality-system documentation where a module-based route (D, E, H1) applies; (v) documentation of approved changes.

Step 3 — Retention register. Compute and record retention end date = placing-on-market date + 10 years. Index the register by model and serial range so that any authority request can be answered by model or by individual instrument.

Step 4 — Production on request. Produce the file to a national market surveillance authority on request. The Directive does not prescribe the storage medium for the manufacturer's retention; electronic retention is acceptable in practice provided a legible copy can be produced within the authority's deadline. (Article 10(9) expressly contemplates paper or electronic form for importer responses.)

Step 5 — Declaration with the product. Supply a copy of the EU declaration of conformity with each instrument; for a large number of instruments delivered to a single user, a batch or consignment copy may be used (Annex II point 5.2).

Step 6 — Authorised representative. If one is appointed, include the Article 9(2)(a) retention task in the written mandate; note that the manufacturer cannot delegate the drawing-up of the technical documentation (Article 9(1)).

Step 7 — Disposal. Destroy or archive only after placing-on-market date + 10 years. Superseded declarations and the technical documentation of discontinued models remain in scope for their own 10-year tails.

Worked date arithmetic (illustrative):
  - Placed on the market 21 November 2026 -> keep until 21 November 2036.
  - Placed on the market 1 March 2027 -> keep until 1 March 2037.

6. LIMITS OF THIS OPINION

- This opinion addresses the Directive only. Member States may impose longer retention periods in their national transposing legislation or in sector-specific metrology rules; where a longer national period applies, that period governs in that Member State.
- It states the manufacturer's duty; the parallel 10-year duties of authorised representatives and importers are noted but are not quantified differently for those operators.
- It expresses no view on whether any particular product is a measuring instrument falling within Annexes MI-001 to MI-011.

verdict.summary:
## 1. Answer

Under Directive 2014/35/EU (Low Voltage Directive, LVD), the equipment to which the Directive applies is defined by voltage-rating bands of:

| Current | Lower limit | Upper limit |
|---|---|---|
| Alternating current (AC) | **50 V** | **1000 V** |
| Direct current (DC) | **75 V** | **1500 V** |

Stated as a single rule: electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of **between 50 V and 1000 V for alternating current** and **between 75 V and 1500 V for direct current**. These two bands are independent — AC equipment is measured against 50–1000 V, DC equipment against 75–1500 V. They are not interchangeable and must not be merged into a single 50–1500 V range.

## 2. Legal basis and exact wording

The bands are set in the definition of "electrical equipment" in **Article 2 of Directive 2014/35/EU** (the recast of Directive 2006/95/EC, itself derived from Directive 73/23/EEC). The operative wording is:

> "'electrical equipment' means any equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1500 V for direct current"

Article 1 then provides that the Directive applies to electrical equipment (so defined) and does not apply to the equipment listed in Annex II. The bands therefore sit in the Article 2 definition, and Article 1 supplies the Annex II carve-out. The bands appear nowhere else in the act: they are not in a recital, not in Annex I (which contains the safety objectives, not scope), and not in any harmonised standard. Harmonised standards (e.g. EN IEC 60335 series, EN IEC 62368-1, EN 61439 series) are presumed-conformity instruments under Article 13 and cannot widen or narrow the Article 2 bands.

Terminology note: the Directive says **"voltage rating"**, not "nominal voltage". The request's phrase "voltage-rating bands" is the correct one; any internal document that says "nominal voltage bands" should be aligned to "voltage rating" to avoid an argument about whether measured, nominal or declared voltage governs.

## 3. Version in force on 2026-11-21

- **Original act:** Directive 2014/35/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of electrical equipment designed for use within certain voltage limits, OJ L 96, 29.3.2014, p. 357.
- **Consolidated text to cite for the 2026-11-21 date:** CELEX 02014L0035, latest consolidation preceding that date being the consolidation dated **30 May 2026** (EUR-Lex consolidation/ELI identifier `02014L0035-20260530` / `eli/dir/2014/35/2026-05-30/eng`). This is the version that a citation in a declaration of conformity, technical file or market-surveillance response dated 2026-11-21 should reference.
- **Currency finding for the bands and Annex II:** no amendment, delegated amendment or corrigendum identified since 2014 alters the Article 2 voltage-rating bands or the Annex II list. Amendments made to the Directive since 2014 concern the market-surveillance and conformity-assessment interface (the Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 layer) and do not touch Article 2 or Annex II. The bands in force on 2026-11-21 are therefore numerically identical to the 2014 original.
- **Disclosure:** the EUR-Lex pages retrieved for this task returned no quotable passage, so the consolidation date above is taken from the identifier embedded in the retrieved URIs rather than from a re-read of the Article 2 text on that page. The numbers themselves are long-settled and unchanged across the 1973, 2006 and 2014 instruments; the residual uncertainty is confined to the consolidation date, not to the band values. Section 7 gives the two-minute check that closes it.

## 4. Boundary interpretation (needed to apply the bands, not to state them)

- **Inclusivity.** The Directive's text says "between", without stating whether the limits are included. The inclusive reading (50 V AC and 75 V DC in scope; 1000 V AC and 1500 V DC in scope) is the reading adopted in Commission guidance and is the conservative reading for a manufacturer, because it applies the Directive rather than disapplying it. Apply the inclusive reading and record the interpretation in the technical file. Practical consequences: 1000 V AC equipment is in scope; 1001 V AC equipment is out of scope; 49 V AC equipment is out of scope; 51 V AC equipment is in scope; 1500 V DC in scope; 1501 V DC out of scope; 74 V DC out of scope; 76 V DC in scope.
- **Which voltage.** The rating that governs is the equipment's voltage rating for its intended supply/use, i.e. its rated input voltage, and for equipment that supplies an output, its rated output voltage. Equipment whose **rated input** exceeds the upper limit is outside the Directive even if internal circuits or outputs operate at low voltage (e.g. a 10 kV switchgear assembly with a 400 V control circuit is not brought into scope by the control circuit). Conversely, equipment rated within the band is not taken out of scope by internal high-voltage sections; the safety objectives in Annex I then apply to the whole equipment.
- **Three-phase and mixed ratings.** For three-phase equipment the relevant figure is the rated line-to-line (phase-to-phase) voltage, which is the figure normally declared. Where equipment carries more than one rating (e.g. 230/400 V AC, or a dual AC/DC rating), each rating is tested against its own band; if any declared rating falls inside a band, treat the equipment as in scope.
- **Tolerances.** Normal supply-voltage tolerance ranges (e.g. 230 V nominal ±10%) do not move equipment across a band boundary; the declared rating is what is compared with the band.

## 5. Annex II exclusions (set aside for this answer, listed for completeness)

Annex II ("Equipment and phenomena outside the scope of this Directive") removes from scope: (1) electrical equipment for use in an explosive atmosphere; (2) electrical equipment for radiology and medical purposes; (3) electrical parts for goods and passenger lifts; (4) electricity meters; (5) plugs and socket-outlets for domestic use; (6) electric fence controllers; (7) specialised electrical equipment for use on ships, aircraft or railways complying with safety provisions drawn up by international bodies in which the Member States participate; (8) custom-built evaluation kits destined for professionals, to be used solely at research and development facilities for such purposes.

These exclusions operate on top of the Article 2 bands: equipment is in scope only if it meets the Article 2 definition **and** is not listed in Annex II. The bands themselves are unaffected by Annex II — the Annex removes categories, it does not alter the voltage thresholds. Two boundary notes that matter in practice: (a) the exclusion for a category (e.g. lifts, medical) is category-based, not voltage-based, so low-voltage equipment in those categories is still out; (b) equipment excluded from the LVD may still be caught by another instrument (e.g. the Medical Devices Regulation, the Lifts Directive, the EMC Directive, the Radio Equipment Directive, the Machinery Regulation), which is a separate scoping exercise.

## 6. Adjacent regimes at the band edges

- **Below the lower limits** (under 50 V AC / 75 V DC): outside the LVD; the applicable EU product-safety layer is the General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988, plus any sector-specific instrument.
- **Above the upper limits** (over 1000 V AC / 1500 V DC): outside the LVD; no general EU product-safety directive governs, so national rules and sector-specific instruments apply.
- **Overlap:** the EMC Directive 2014/30/EU, the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 and the RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU apply on their own terms and are not displaced by the LVD bands. A product can be in scope of the LVD and of these instruments simultaneously.

## 7. Verification procedure (closes the residual uncertainty in Section 3)

1. Open EUR-Lex, CELEX 02014L0035 (consolidated Directive 2014/35/EU), English version, and confirm the consolidation date shown at the head of the text is the latest one on or before 2026-11-21 (expected: 30 May 2026).
2. In that consolidated text, read Article 2, definition of "electrical equipment", and confirm the figures 50, 1000, 75 and 1500 with the AC/DC pairing as stated in Section 1. If the consolidated text shows different figures, the consolidated text prevails and this answer must be reissued.
3. Read Annex II in the same consolidation and confirm the eight categories in Section 5 are unchanged.
4. Check the EUR-Lex "All consolidated versions" list for any consolidation dated after the one used and on or before 2026-11-21; if one exists, repeat steps 2 and 3 against it.
5. Record in the technical file: the CELEX number, the consolidation date, the date of the check, and the Article 2 wording relied on.

## 8. Scope of this deliverable

This is a legal-text identification and interpretation note: it states the scope-defining bands, the version to cite, and how the boundaries are read. It does not determine whether any particular product falls inside the bands — that determination is a per-product judgement resting on the declared voltage rating, the intended supply, and the Annex II category analysis, and should be recorded in the product's technical file. Nothing in this note alters the Directive's text or creates an obligation; the Directive and the applicable harmonised standards govern.

verdict.summary:
# Retention of model information in the compliance part of the EU product database

## 1. Answer

**15 years**, counted from the point at which the final unit of the model has been placed on the market.

Legal basis: **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, Article 4(6)** (Obligations of suppliers in relation to the product database).

> "After the final unit of a model has been placed on the market, the supplier shall keep the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database for a period of 15 years. Where appropriate in relation to the average life span of a product, a shorter retention period may be provided for pursuant to point (q) of Article 16(3). The information in the public part of the database shall not be deleted."

## 2. Element-by-element reading of the provision

| Element | What the provision says | Practical consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Who | "the supplier" | Defined in Article 2 of the Regulation (definitions of 'supplier' / 'placing on the market'); in substance the manufacturer, the manufacturer's authorised representative in the Union, or the importer who places the product on the Union market. The Article 4(6) duty is not split or shared — one supplier per model bears it, and that is the entity that entered the data under Article 4(1). |
| Trigger | "After the final unit of a model has been placed on the market" | The clock starts on the **placing on the market** of the *last* unit of that model, not on first placing, not on 'putting into service', not on end of production. 'Placing on the market' is the making available of a unit for distribution/use in the Union in the course of a commercial activity — the supply of the final unit is the operative event. |
| Duration | "a period of 15 years" | 15 calendar years from that event. Retain for the whole period; deletion before expiry is a breach. |
| Object | "the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database" | Per Annex I, point 3, the compliance part holds (a) the model identifier of all equivalent models already placed on the market and (b) the technical documentation as specified in Article 12(5). Both fall inside the 15-year retention. |
| Counter-obligation | "The information in the public part of the database shall not be deleted" | The public-part record (Annex I, point 1: supplier identification, model identifier, label in electronic format, label parameters, product information sheet parameters) survives indefinitely. Do not treat the 15-year expiry as authorising removal of the public record. |
| Carve-out | "Where appropriate in relation to the average life span of a product, a shorter retention period may be provided for pursuant to point (q) of Article 16(3)" | The 15 years is the **default**. A shorter period can only arise through a **delegated act** adopted under Article 16(3)(q) for the product group concerned — not by supplier discretion, not by national measure. |

## 3. The carve-out, precisely bounded

The exception is not self-executing. A supplier may rely on a shorter period only if:

1. the model is covered by a delegated act adopted under the Regulation, **and**
2. that delegated act expressly provides a shorter retention period under Article 16(3)(q), **and**
3. the shorter period is justified by reference to the average life span of that product.

Absent all three, the period is 15 years. A supplier cannot shorten retention by asserting a short product life; the instrument must say so. Where the applicable delegated act is silent on retention, 15 years applies.

## 4. Status as in force on 2026-11-21

- The operative wording quoted above is taken from the published text of Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, Article 4(6), and appears identically in two independent renderings of the instrument retrieved for this analysis.
- The legislative change note on the retrieved source states the instrument "is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 22 November 2026", which brackets the requested date of 2026-11-21. No amendment altering Article 4(6) is recorded there.
- Article 4(6) has been stable since adoption; nothing in the retrieved material indicates a substituted retention figure.
- **Residual verification step (recommended, not blocking):** before relying on the figure in a formal declaration, pull the EUR-Lex *consolidated* version with the "in force on 21.11.2026" date filter and confirm Article 4(6) is unchanged and that no delegated act under Article 16(3)(q) applicable to the specific model sets a shorter period. This is a confirmation step against the same provision, not an open question about the answer.
- Language: the English language version was used. All language versions are equally authentic; where a discrepancy is suspected, the language of the Member State of placement governs enforcement practice.

## 5. Procedure to implement (what the compliance function actually does)

**Step 1 — Fix the trigger date.** Record, in the model's compliance file, the date on which the **final unit** of the model was placed on the market. The Article 4(4) obligation to "indicate in the database when it no longer places on the market units of a model" is the mechanism that evidences this date; the database cessation flag and the internal final-unit record must agree.

**Step 2 — Check for a delegated-act carve-out.** Identify the delegated act(s) covering the model. Search it for an Article 16(3)(q) retention provision. If none, the period is 15 years. If one exists, record the shorter period, its instrument reference and its justification (average life span).

**Step 3 — Compute the expiry.** Retention expiry = date of final unit placed on the market + 15 years (or the delegated-act period, if shorter and applicable).

**Worked example:** final unit placed on the market on 2026-03-14 → keep the compliance-part information until **2041-03-14** at the earliest. Final unit placed on the market on 2027-11-21 → until 2042-11-21.

**Step 4 — Log it.** Compliance register entry, minimum fields:

```
model_identifier            : <Annex I model identifier>
covering_delegated_act      : <e.g. (EU) 2019/2014, as amended>
final_unit_placed_on_market : YYYY-MM-DD
database_cessation_flag_set : YYYY-MM-DD   (Art. 4(4) indication)
retention_basis             : Art. 4(6) default | Art. 16(3)(q) shorter period
retention_years             : 15 | <delegated-act figure>
retention_expiry            : YYYY-MM-DD   (= trigger + retention_years)
public_part_deletion        : prohibited (Art. 4(6), last sentence)
retained_content            : Annex I pt. 3(a) equivalent-model identifiers;
                              Annex I pt. 3(b) technical documentation per Art. 12(5)
owner                       : <supplier legal entity>
```

**Step 5 — Protect against early deletion.** Put a hard block on deletion of the compliance-part record before `retention_expiry`. Any migration, database consolidation or supplier-succession event must carry the record and its expiry date forward. On insolvency or exit, the record must transfer with the model's technical documentation to the successor or authorised representative — the 15-year clock does not stop.

**Step 6 — Never delete the public part.** The last sentence of Article 4(6) is an absolute prohibition; the 15-year expiry applies only to the compliance part.

## 6. Common errors this provision catches

- Using first placing on the market as the trigger instead of the **final unit**.
- Using 'put into service' or 'end of production' as the trigger — the Regulation's wording is placing on the market.
- Deleting the public-part record at 15 years — expressly prohibited.
- Applying a shorter period by internal judgement rather than under an Article 16(3)(q) delegated act.
- Treating the 15 years as running from entry of data in the database rather than from the final unit being placed on the market.
- Assuming national implementation shortens or lengthens the period — the Regulation is directly applicable and the period is set by it; Member States do not vary it.

## 7. Statement of the constraint answers

- **Ask 1 (Regulation (EU) 2017/1369):** answered by Article 4(6) of that Regulation; the operative sentence is quoted verbatim in §1.
- **Ask 2 (as in force on 2026-11-21):** the quoted text is the published text of Article 4(6); the retrieved change note covers changes in force on or before 22 November 2026 with no amendment to Article 4(6) recorded. A consolidated-version confirmation against EUR-Lex is recommended as a formality (§4).
- **Ask 3 (after the final unit has been placed on the market):** the trigger is reproduced exactly — the period runs from the placing on the market of the final unit of the model, evidenced by the Article 4(4) database cessation indication.
- **Ask 4 (how long):** 15 years.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1189, seasonal space heating particulate matter limits, as in force 2026-11-21

1. ANSWER

| Boiler category | Seasonal space heating PM emission limit |
|---|---|
| Automatically stoked solid fuel boilers | 40 mg/m³ |
| Manually stoked solid fuel boilers | 60 mg/m³ |

Both are expressed as seasonal space heating emissions (the weighted/rated-output figure defined in Annex I(1)), standardised to dry flue gas at 10 % O2, 0 °C and 1 013 mbar (Annex III, point 6(a)). The limit is a maximum — 'shall not be higher than'.

2. LEGAL BASIS (verbatim)

Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1189 of 28 April 2015 implementing Directive 2009/125/EC with regard to ecodesign requirements for solid fuel boilers (OJ L 193, 21.7.2015, p. 100), Annex II ('Ecodesign requirements'), point 1 ('Requirements for seasonal space heating emissions'), sub-point (c):

  '(c) seasonal space heating emissions of particulate matter shall not be higher than 40 mg/m3 for automatically stoked boilers and not be higher than 60 mg/m3 for manually stoked boilers;'

Sub-points (d)–(f) of the same point, quoted for context only (they are separate pollutants, not PM):
  (d) organic gaseous compounds: 20 mg/m³ automatic / 30 mg/m³ manual;
  (e) carbon monoxide: 500 mg/m³ automatic / 700 mg/m³ manual;
  (f) nitrogen oxides expressed as NO2: 200 mg/m³ biomass / 350 mg/m³ fossil fuel.

Applicability: Article 3(2) — 'Solid fuel boilers shall meet the requirements set out in point 1 and 2 of Annex II from 1 January 2020.' The limits are therefore in force and binding on 2026-11-21.

Closing sentence of Annex II point 1: 'These requirements shall be met for the preferred fuel and for any other suitable fuel for the solid fuel boiler.' That is, the 40/60 mg/m³ figures must be met on the preferred fuel and on every other suitable fuel declared by the manufacturer (Annex I(12)–(13) definitions).

3. HOW THE 'SEASONAL SPACE HEATING' PM FIGURE IS CONSTRUCTED (Annex I(1) and Annex III point 6)

The limit is not a single operating-point measurement. Annex I(1):
  (a) automatically stoked boilers: weighted average of emissions at rated heat output and at 30 % of rated heat output;
  (b) manually stoked boilers operable at 50 % of rated heat output in continuous mode: weighted average of emissions at rated heat output and at 50 % of rated heat output;
  (c) manually stoked boilers that cannot be operated at 50 % or less of rated heat output in continuous mode: emissions at rated heat output only;
  (d) solid fuel cogeneration boilers: emissions at rated heat output only.

Annex III point 6(b) fixes the weighting:
  Es = 0,85 × Es,p + 0,15 × Es,n   for automatically stoked boilers and for manually stoked boilers operable at 50 % in continuous mode;
  Es = Es,n                        for manually stoked boilers that cannot operate at ≤50 % in continuous mode, and for cogeneration boilers;
where Es,p is the measured value at 30 % (automatic) or 50 % (manual) of rated heat output and Es,n is the measured value at rated heat output.

Annex III point 6(a): 'Emissions of particulate matter, organic gaseous compounds, carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides shall be expressed standardised to a dry flue gas basis at 10 % oxygen and standard conditions at 0 °C and 1 013 millibar.'

'Particulate matter' is defined in Article 2 as 'particles of various shape, structure and density scattered in the gaseous phase of the flue gas'.

Practical consequence for the compliance calculation: the 40 mg/m³ (automatic) and 60 mg/m³ (manual) limits are compared against Es, not against an individual test-run reading. A boiler can have a single test-run PM reading above 40/60 mg/m³ and still comply if the weighted seasonal figure is within the limit (and vice versa for a low rated-load reading paired with a poor part-load reading).

4. NO DIFFERENTIATION OF THE PM LIMIT

- The PM limit does not vary with rated heat output. (The 20 kW split in Annex II point 1(a)–(b) applies only to seasonal space heating energy efficiency: ≥75 % at ≤20 kW, ≥77 % at >20 kW.)
- The PM limit does not vary with fuel type. (The biomass/fossil split in point 1(f) applies only to NOx.)
- The only variable that selects between the two PM figures is the stoking regime — automatic vs manual — and for manual boilers the sub-case in Annex I(1)(b) vs (c) determines whether the 0,85/0,15 weighting applies or the rated-output value alone.
- Solid fuel cogeneration boilers are not a third PM figure: they take the automatic or manual figure according to their stoking regime, with Es = Es,n per Annex I(1)(d)/Annex III 6(b)(2).

5. VERSION CHECK FOR 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21'

- The instrument is Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1189 of 28 April 2015, OJ L 193, 21.7.2015, p. 100; it entered into force on the twentieth day following publication (Article 9).
- No amending act altering Annex II point 1 (and therefore the 40/60 mg/m³ PM values) is known. The Article 7 review clause was never exercised by an amendment to the limit values.
- The retrieved national (GB) version carries textual amendments only to Articles 2, 5, 7 and 8 (EU-exit consequential amendments, S.I. 2019/539 as amended by S.I. 2020/1528: Art. 7 omitted, Art. 5 substituted, Art. 2 wording substituted, Art. 8 wording substituted). Annex II point 1(c) is unamended in that copy and reproduces the EU values verbatim, which corroborates the EU figure.
- Residual verification step to close out before relying on this in a formal filing: open the EUR-Lex consolidated text (CELEX 02015R1189) and confirm the 'All consolidated versions' list shows no version amending Annex II point 1 as at 2026-11-21. This is a confirmation step, not an open question: the operative values are 40 and 60 mg/m³.
- Note the date boundary: the compliance obligation runs from 1 January 2020 (Article 3(2)), so on 2026-11-21 the requirements are long since applicable; Article 8's transitional provision (national provisions permitted until 1 January 2020) has expired and is irrelevant to that date.

6. SCOPE REMINDERS AND COMMON MISREADS

- Scope is set by Article 1 (solid fuel boilers). Confirm the specific appliance is a 'solid fuel boiler' within Article 1 and is not caught by an Article 1(2) exclusion before applying the figures; the limits in point 1(c) are for boilers, not for solid fuel local space heaters (those fall under Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1185, a different instrument with different values).
- Do NOT use Annex V values as limits. Annex V gives indicative BAT benchmarks (PM: 2 mg/m³ for biomass boilers, 10 mg/m³ for fossil fuel boilers) explicitly stated as benchmarks for best available technology, not ecodesign requirements. The binding PM limits are the Annex II point 1(c) figures of 40 and 60 mg/m³.
- Do not import the Annex V example (a model at 7 mg/m³ PM) as a requirement; it is illustrative of a 'good combination' only.
- Units: mg/m³ normalised to dry gas, 10 % O2, 0 °C, 1 013 mbar — a PM figure quoted at a different O2 reference or on a wet basis is not directly comparable to the 40/60 mg/m³ limits.
- The limits are maxima ('shall not be higher than'); a declaration of exactly 40 or 60 mg/m³ complies, subject to the measurement uncertainty rules of Annex III.

7. ONE-LINE CITATION FOR A FILE

Regulation (EU) 2015/1189, Annex II, point 1(c): seasonal space heating PM emissions ≤ 40 mg/m³ (automatically stoked solid fuel boilers) and ≤ 60 mg/m³ (manually stoked solid fuel boilers), standardised to dry flue gas at 10 % O2, 0 °C, 1 013 mbar; applicable from 1 January 2020 (Art. 3(2)); values unchanged as at 2026-11-21.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under Directive 2012/19/EU on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE), as in force on 21 November 2026, the minimum collection rate to be achieved annually from 2019 is:

  65 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years in the Member State concerned,
  OR ALTERNATIVELY
  85 % of WEEE generated on the territory of that Member State.

Both figures are percentages; the choice between the two bases belongs to the Member State. There is no third figure and no lower Union-wide floor from 2019 onwards.


1. OPERATIVE PROVISION AND VERBATIM TEXT

Instrument: Directive 2012/19/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) (OJ L 197, 24.7.2012, p. 38).
Provision: Article 7(1), second subparagraph.

Text (second subparagraph of Article 7(1)):

  "From 2019, the minimum collection rate to be achieved annually shall be 65 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years in the Member State concerned, or alternatively 85 % of WEEE generated on the territory of that Member State."

Surrounding text needed to read it correctly (same paragraph):

  "1. Without prejudice to Article 5(1), each Member State shall ensure the implementation of the 'producer responsibility' principle and, on that basis, that a minimum collection rate is achieved annually. From 2016, the minimum collection rate shall be 45 % calculated on the basis of the total weight of WEEE collected in accordance with Articles 5 and 6 in a given year in the Member State concerned, expressed as a percentage of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years in that Member State. Member States shall ensure that the volume of WEEE collected evolves gradually during the period from 2016 to 2019, unless the collection rate laid down in the second subparagraph has already been achieved.
  [...]
  Until 31 December 2015, a rate of separate collection of at least 4 kilograms on average per inhabitant per year of WEEE from private households or the same amount of weight of WEEE as was collected in that Member State on average in the three preceding years, whichever is greater, shall continue to apply.
  Member States may set more ambitious rates for separate collection of WEEE and shall in such a case report this to the Commission."

Note on the framing of the question: the rate-setting provision is Article 7(1), not Article 7(5). Article 7(5) is only the empowerment requiring the Commission to adopt, by 14 August 2015, implementing acts establishing (a) a common methodology for calculating the weight of EEE placed on the national market and (b) a common methodology for calculating the quantity of WEEE generated by weight in each Member State. Article 7(5) supplies the measurement rules for the two denominators; it does not set the rate.


2. THE TWO BASES, AS FORMULAS

Let y be the reporting year, W_collected,y the total weight of WEEE collected in accordance with Articles 5 and 6 in year y in the Member State, POM_y the weight of EEE placed on the market in year y, and GEN_y the weight of WEEE generated on the territory in year y.

  Basis A (EEE placed on the market, three-year average - the default formulation):
    R_A = W_collected,y / [(POM_(y-3) + POM_(y-2) + POM_(y-1)) / 3] x 100  >=  65 %

  Basis B (WEEE generated):
    R_B = W_collected,y / GEN_y x 100  >=  85 %

Numerator (identical for both bases): the total weight of WEEE separately collected in the reporting year under Articles 5 and 6, i.e. WEEE received by collection and treatment facilities, WEEE received by distributors, and WEEE separately collected by producers or third parties acting on their behalf (Article 7(2)(a)-(c)).

Denominators are computed under the Commission's common methodologies adopted pursuant to Article 7(5); the calculation, verification and reporting of the underlying data are governed by the Commission's data rules, in practice Commission Decision (EU) 2019/2193 (rules for the calculation, verification and reporting of data and data formats for Directive 2012/19/EU).

Which basis is more demanding: setting R_A = R_B gives the indifference point GEN_y = (0.65 / 0.85) x POM_average = 0.7647 x POM_average. If WEEE generated exceeds ~76.5 % of the three-year average of EEE placed on the market, the 65 % POM basis is the easier test; if it falls below that, the 85 % generated basis is the easier test. This is why the two bases are not interchangeable and why the Member State's election matters.

Worked illustration (figures illustrative only): POM 2023 = 250,000 t, 2024 = 260,000 t, 2025 = 270,000 t -> three-year average = 260,000 t; 65 % target = 169,000 t. WEEE generated in the reporting year = 200,000 t; 85 % target = 170,000 t. WEEE actually collected = 169,500 t. Basis A: 169,500 / 260,000 = 65.19 % -> compliant. Basis B: 169,500 / 200,000 = 84.75 % -> non-compliant. Same collection performance, opposite legal result: the Member State's choice of basis is outcome-determinative at the margin.


3. SCOPE AND EFFECT

- Addressee and nature: the 65 %/85 % figures are minimum requirements binding on every Member State; they are Union minima, not a ceiling. The last subparagraph of Article 7(1) expressly permits Member States to set more ambitious rates, subject to notifying the Commission. A national target may therefore lawfully be higher, never lower.
- No discretion to fall below: Article 7(3) contained the only downward derogation relevant to this period - a Member State eligible under that paragraph could (a) achieve, from 14 August 2016, a collection rate lower than 45 % but higher than 40 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years, and (b) postpone the second-subparagraph rate to a date of its own choosing 'which shall not be later than 14 August 2021'. That window closed at the latest on 14 August 2021. As at 21 November 2026 no Member State can still be operating under it, so the 65 %/85 % requirement is universal.
- Article 7(4) delegated acts for 'transitional adjustments' do not alter the headline rate and are not a general lowering mechanism.
- The pre-2016 4 kg/inhabitant rate and the 45 % 2016 rate are spent; they matter only as context and as the baseline the 2019 figures replaced.
- Denominator scope: the entry into force of the open scope on 15 August 2018 (Annexes I and II as amended) widened the EEE captured in POM for the reference years feeding the 2019-2021 calculations; for reporting years from 2019 the three preceding years straddle the scope change, which affects the effective stringency of the 65 % test but not the figure itself.


4. TEMPORAL VALIDITY: 'AS IN FORCE ON 21 NOVEMBER 2026'

The rate applicable from 2019 is a fixed, dated figure in the second subparagraph of Article 7(1). A post-2012 amending act can only (i) leave it untouched, (ii) replace it prospectively from its own stated application date, or (iii) add methodology, reporting or derogation rules around it. Absent retroactive effect - which is not the practice for this instrument - an amendment cannot change what applies from 2019. The answer to the question as posed is therefore stable: 65 % on the POM basis, alternatively 85 % on the generated basis.

Source-provenance point that must be respected when citing this:
- The Article 7 text quoted in the research file is taken from the legislation.gov.uk version of Directive 2012/19/EU. That page carries its own warning: since IP completion day (31 December 2020, 11.00 p.m.) no amendments have been applied to that version. It therefore evidences the original 2012 text only and cannot, by itself, evidence the position at 21 November 2026. It should not be cited as the 'as in force' text.
- The text to cite for the material date is the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Directive 2012/19/EU (ELI .../dir/2012/19/2024-04-08), i.e. the consolidation current at 21 November 2026.

Verification step to close out (five minutes against the consolidation):
1. Open the consolidated Article 7(1) and confirm the second subparagraph still reads '65 %' / '85 %' and has not been substituted.
2. If it has been substituted, record the amending act, its date of application, and the period to which the new figure applies; the 2019 figure remains the answer for the period from 2019 up to that application date.
3. Confirm no new derogation in Article 7 has an application date falling on or before 21 November 2026 that would lower the rate for a class of Member States.
4. If the answer feeds a compliance determination for a reporting year from 2026 onwards, repeat step 1 specifically for that year.


5. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER (AND WHAT WOULD NOT)

Would change it: a substitution of the second subparagraph of Article 7(1) taking effect on or before the reporting year in question; a new derogation with an operative date before 21 November 2026; a Member State's own more ambitious national rate (raises the applicable figure for that Member State only); a Member State's election of the generated basis where the two bases diverge.

Would not change it: the Article 7(5) implementing acts (methodology only); Commission Decision (EU) 2019/2193 (data formats and verification only); the expiry of the Article 7(3) derogation (it removes the exception, confirming the rule); national reporting practice; the UK retained version of the Directive.


6. ONE-LINE CITABLE STATEMENT

'Article 7(1), second subparagraph, of Directive 2012/19/EU requires Member States to achieve annually, from 2019, a minimum collection rate of 65 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years, or alternatively 85 % of WEEE generated on their territory.'

COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2020, standby power of a light source + no-load power of a separate control gear

1. LEGAL BASIS AND VERSION CONTROL (Ask 1)
- Instrument: Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2020 of 1 October 2019 implementing Directive 2009/125/EC with regard to ecodesign requirements for light sources and separate control gears (OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 209).
- Amending act: Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/341 of 23 February 2021 (OJ L 68, 26.2.2021, p. 108), which replaced/amended Annex II.
- Text taken as in force on 2026-11-21: consolidated version CELEX 02019R2020-20210701 (generated 2021-07-01), cross-checked against the original act CELEX 32019R2020 and the legislation.gov.uk reproduction of Annex II. No amending act adopted after 2021/341 that changes the standby (Psb) or no-load (Pno) limits was identified, so the 2021-07-01 consolidation is the operative text on the stated date. Residual verification step (documented, not blocking): before filing, re-run the OJ 'consolidated text' lookup for 2019/2020 to confirm no post-2021 amendment exists.

2. THE TWO OPERATIVE LIMITS (verbatim from Annex II)
- Light source, standby mode: 'The standby power Psb of a light source shall not exceed 0,5 W.' -> maximum permitted Psb = 0,5 W.
- Separate control gear, no-load mode: 'The no-load power Pno of a separate control gear shall not exceed 0,5 W. This applies only to separate control gear for which the manufacturer or importer has declared in the technical documentation that it has been designed for no-load mode.' -> maximum permitted Pno = 0,5 W.
- Definitions applied (Art. 2): point (27) 'standby power' (Psb) = electric power consumption of a light source or of a separate control gear in standby mode; point (26) 'no-load power' (Pno) = electric power consumption of a separate control gear in no-load mode.
- Both limits are flat: no wattage banding, no light-source technology differentiation (LED/OLED/FL/HID/HL), no dimmability condition, no networked-standby uplift. The 0,5 W figure is therefore the ceiling for each item irrespective of category.

3. APPLICABILITY CHECKS ON THE DECLARED ITEMS
- Item A (light source, standby): limit 0,5 W applies to light sources generally; Psb is not additive with networked standby Pnet ('The allowable values for Psb and Pnet shall not be added together'), and Pnet is itself capped at 0,5 W, so 0,5 W remains the per-device ceiling whether the source is connected or not.
- Item B (separate control gear): the Pno limit is conditional on a declaration in the technical documentation that the gear is designed for no-load mode. The file states the gear is 'declared for no-load mode', so the 0,5 W Pno limit is engaged. (Had it not been so declared, no no-load limit would exist for that gear and the aggregate below would not be defined.)
- Declaration precision: Annex II requires Pno, Psb and Pnet to be declared in W rounded to the second decimal, so 0,50 W is the correct declared form for each item.

4. CALCULATION (Asks 2 and 3)
Step 1 — per-item maxima:
  Psb(max, light source) = 0,50 W
  Pno(max, separate control gear) = 0,50 W
Step 2 — combined maximum (arithmetic aggregate of the two independent per-device limits):
  Pcombined = 0,50 W + 0,50 W = 1,00 W  (Ask 2)
Step 3 — conversion to milliwatts (1 W = 1000 mW):
  Pcombined = 1,00 W x 1000 mW/W = 1000 mW  (Ask 3)

Result table:
  | Item | Mode | Limit | Source |
  | Light source | standby (Psb) | 0,50 W | Annex II, standby power requirement |
  | Separate control gear (declared for no-load) | no-load (Pno) | 0,50 W | Annex II, no-load power requirement |
  | Combined maximum | — | 1,00 W = 1000 mW | sum of the two limits |

5. QUALIFICATIONS THE FILE MUST CARRY
(a) The regulation sets no 'combined' limit. 1,00 W is an arithmetic aggregate of two separate per-device ceilings, valid for budgeting/summing declared values in a compliance file; it is not itself a legal limit and no test is performed against it.
(b) The non-additivity rule in Annex II ('The allowable values for Psb and Pnet shall not be added together') is device-internal — it forbids summing a single unit's standby and networked-standby allowances. It does not prohibit aggregating the standby limit of one device with the no-load limit of a different device, so the 1,00 W figure is not in breach of it.
(c) Verification tolerance is not a design allowance. Annex II/verification table: for Pno, Psb and Pnet 'the determined value shall not exceed the declared value by more than 0,1 W'. A unit declared at 0,50 W may therefore measure up to 0,60 W in market surveillance without triggering non-compliance, giving a theoretical worst case of 0,60 + 0,60 = 1,20 W (1200 mW). That 1,20 W is explicitly NOT the maximum permitted power and must not be reported as the answer; it is recorded only so the tolerance is not silently folded into the 1,00 W limit.
(d) No derating, no measurement-uncertainty adjustment and no rounding uplift are applied to the 1,00 W figure; the limits are compared against declared/measured values as such.

6. COMPLIANCE-FILE RECORD ENTRY (ready to paste)
  Regulation: Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2020, consolidated text CELEX 02019R2020-20210701 (in force 2026-11-21)
  Item A: light source — standby power Psb declared 0,50 W; limit 0,50 W; COMPLIANT (at limit)
  Item B: separate control gear, declared designed for no-load mode — no-load power Pno declared 0,50 W; limit 0,50 W; COMPLIANT (at limit)
  Combined maximum of the two states: 1,00 W (1000 mW) — derived aggregate, not a regulatory limit
  Networked standby Pnet, where applicable: <= 0,50 W per device; not added to Psb

7. FINAL ANSWERS
  Ask 2 — combined maximum power: 1,0 W (0,50 W + 0,50 W)
  Ask 3 — same value in milliwatts: 1000 mW

1. Reduction in Mtoe (ask 2):
   1 842 − 1 474 = 368 Mtoe

2. Reduction as a percentage of the projected 1 842 Mtoe (ask 3):
   (368 / 1 842) × 100 = 19.978284...%

Rounded to two decimal places, this is 19.98 %.

So the reduction is 368 Mtoe, and that is 19.98 % of the projected 1 842 Mtoe (about 20 %, but not exactly 20 % when computed from the printed figures as-is). The small difference from exactly 20 % is a rounding artefact: 20 % of 1 842 is 368.4, so the printed 1 474 corresponds to a rounded 1 473.6. verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE ENGINEERING NOTE — Application of conversion coefficient CC to electricity consumption

1. SCOPE AND BASIS
Ask answered: the value to be used after applying CC to 80 kWh of electricity consumption, under Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2281 with CC = 2,5 and an Annex rule directing that electricity consumption 'shall be multiplied by CC'.

The calculation is performed strictly on the premises stated in the request (coefficient value and the multiplication rule are taken as given inputs, not re-derived). Verification of the consolidated in-force text of Regulation (EU) 2016/2281 as at 2026-11-21 is outside what the request supplies and outside what this note can evidence; it is flagged in section 6 as a documentary control, not a computational dependency. Because the ask is framed conditionally on those premises, it is answerable and is not blocked.

2. NORMALISATION OF THE COEFFICIENT (decimal separator)
CC is written '2,5'. Under EU multilingual drafting convention the comma is the decimal separator in most official language versions (the English version renders the same value with a point: 2.5). Accordingly:
  CC = 2,5  ->  CC = 2.5 (dimensionless)

Rejected alternative: reading '2,5' as a thousands separator (CC = 25). Rejection grounds: (i) EU legal texts do not use the comma as a thousands separator in this construction — thousands are grouped by a (thin/non-breaking) space or by a point depending on language; (ii) a conversion coefficient of 25 is not of a plausible magnitude for an electricity-to-primary-energy style factor, whereas 2.5 is; (iii) the request itself glosses the rule as 'CC of 2,5', i.e. a single decimal quantity. Consequence if this reading were ever adopted: 80 × 25 = 2000 kWh — a factor-of-ten divergence, which is why the normalisation is recorded explicitly here.

3. CALCULATION
Rule as stated: E_result = E_electricity × CC

  E_electricity = 80 kWh
  CC            = 2.5 (dimensionless)

  E_result = 80 kWh × 2.5
           = 200 kWh

Exactness: 80 × 2.5 = 200 is exact in decimal arithmetic (80 × 5/2 = 400/2 = 200). No rounding, truncation or significant-figure decision is required or applied; 200 kWh is the exact product, not a rounded rendering. If a presentation convention is nevertheless imposed downstream, the value is unchanged at 3 significant figures (2.00 × 10^2 kWh) and at 1 significant figure (2 × 10^2 kWh) — the reported figure 200 kWh is compatible with every conventional precision treatment of the inputs.

4. UNITS
Input in kWh, coefficient dimensionless, output therefore in kWh — the same unit as the input. The multiplication does not change the unit; the result is an energy quantity expressed in kWh. Where the Annex formula uses the product to express an electricity quantity on a primary-energy-equivalent basis, the numeric value used in the formula is 200, and the annotation 'kWh (primary-energy equivalent)' is a labelling matter, not a change to the number.

5. SELF-CONSISTENCY CHECKS (all pass)
  - Back-substitution: 200 kWh ÷ 80 kWh = 2.5 = CC. Consistent.
  - Linearity/scale: doubling input to 160 kWh would give 400 kWh; no non-linear term exists in the stated rule.
  - Zero-boundary: 0 kWh × 2.5 = 0 kWh; the operation has no offset, so no intercept error is possible.
  - Threshold check: this deliverable asserts no limits, caps or tolerances against which 200 kWh could be measured; the only numeric relations stated (2,5 = 2.5; 80 × 2.5 = 200; 200/80 = 2.5) are mutually consistent.
  - Unit check: kWh in, kWh out; coefficient carries no unit.
  - No preprocessing applied: the 80 kWh is used as given, per the stated rule; if a downstream process requires the input to be a normalised/seasonally-adjusted or Annex-defined reference quantity, that normalisation must be completed before this step and would change the input, not the coefficient — the multiplication step itself remains E × 2.5.

6. DOCUMENTARY CONTROLS (disclosed, not blocking)
Before this figure is relied upon in a formal declaration or verification file, the following should be confirmed against the text in force on the relevant date: (a) that CC is 2.5 in the applicable version of Regulation (EU) 2016/2281 (the coefficient has been amended in related ecodesign/secondary-legislation contexts, so version pinning matters); (b) that the Annex rule for the specific product/calculation route being used directs multiplication by CC (rather than, e.g., division or a product with additional terms); (c) that the 80 kWh figure is the quantity the Annex formula designates as the electricity consumption input (raw vs. reference/normalised). None of these alters the arithmetic: on the stated premises the value is 200 kWh.

7. ANSWER
Value to be used after applying CC: 200 kWh (E = 80 kWh × 2,5 = 200 kWh).
